# Documents in a relational database

Sooner or later most applications need a bit of schemaless data, such as attributes that differ
per row or a payload stored exactly as it arrived. `JSONB` lets a Postgres column hold a whole JSON
document, stored in a binary form that can be indexed, next to ordinary typed columns. That covers
the need without a second database. The SQL takes half a dozen operators, and SQLAlchemy maps each
of them to Python.

## Reading values out

Four operators cover most reads. The first two take a key and differ in what they return, because
`->` gives back JSON and `->>` gives back text.

| SQL | SQLAlchemy | result |
|---|---|---|
| `payload -> 'k'` | `Event.payload["k"]` | jsonb |
| `payload ->> 'k'` | `Event.payload["k"].astext` | text |
| `payload #>> '{a,b}'` | `Event.payload[("a", "b")].astext` | text, nested |
| `(payload ->> 'k')::int` | `Event.payload["k"].as_integer()` | integer |

A missing key comes back as SQL `NULL`. That small rule matters more than it looks, as the next
section shows.

## Filtering, and the NULL trap

Most filters use containment, `@>`, which asks whether the document includes a given fragment. A
GIN index (an index over the keys and values inside each document) can serve it.

```python
select(Event).where(Event.payload.contains({"user": {"plan": "pro"}}))
```

The trap is negation. `payload ->> 'device' != 'web'` silently drops every row that has no `device`
key at all. For those rows the left side is `NULL`, and `NULL != 'web'` is not true but `NULL`.
When a missing key should count as "not web", the query has to say so, as in
`or_(Event.payload["device"].astext != "web", ~Event.payload.has_key("device"))`.

## Arrays become rows

`jsonb_array_elements` turns one row that holds an array into one row per element. From there,
`WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `JOIN` work as usual. In SQLAlchemy, `.table_valued(...)` turns the function
into something you can put in `FROM`. You then join it `ON true`, and Postgres evaluates the join
laterally, once per row. In code it looks like this:

```python
item = func.jsonb_array_elements(Event.payload["items"]).table_valued(column("value", JSONB))
select(Event.id, item.c.value["sku"].astext).join(item, true())
```

`jsonb_to_recordset` does the same but returns typed columns instead of one `jsonb` value. When the
elements share a shape, that saves the casts.

## Paths and updates

Postgres 12 added the SQL/JSON path language, a small query language that runs inside one document
and is a close cousin of `jq`. For example, `$.items[*] ? (@.qty > 1)` selects the items with a
quantity above one.

Updates are operators too. `||` merges two documents, `-` removes a key, `#-` removes a path, and
`jsonb_set` writes a value at a path. Add `RETURNING` and the same round trip sends back what
changed.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When JSONB, when columns

Use columns for anything you filter, join or aggregate on routinely. Use JSONB for the long tail,
such as attributes that differ per row, payloads you store as received, and settings. A GIN index with
`jsonb_path_ops` makes containment fast, but no index makes a JSONB key as cheap to query as a
typed column.
:::
